The PKGBUILD only contains variable declarations and a `pkgver()` function that extracts version information from a control file within the source archive. The `pkgver()` function runs `bsdtar -xf control.tar.xz` and `cat control`, which assume the archive has been extracted; these operations are local file reads and pose no network or command execution risk. The source is fetched from the official upstream domain (`mediahuman.com`) with a pinned SHA256 checksum. There are no obfuscated, encoded, or command-injection patterns. No dangerous commands like `eval`, `curl|bash`, or network exfiltration are present. The narrow gate operations (fetching sources and sourcing the PKGBUILD) are safe.
</details>

LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This PKGBUILD is a straightforward binary package wrapper. It downloads the vendor's official `.deb` from `https://www.mediahuman.com/de/download/YouTubeToMP3.amd64.deb`, verifies it against a pinned SHA-256 checksum, extracts the `data.tar.xz` into `pkgdir`, installs the copyright file, and creates a symlink for the executable. The `pkgver()` function extracts and reads the `Version:` field from the `.deb` to derive the package version — a routine, non-executed string read that poses no risk.

There is no obfuscated code, no encoded/assembled commands, no network fetch-and-execute pattern, no write outside `$pkgdir`/`$srcdir`, and no exfiltration of local data. The only network destination is the upstream vendor's own download URL, and the checksum is pinned, which is good packaging hygiene. The use of `bsdtar` against the package's declared source is normal for extracting `.deb` contents. No genuinely malicious behavior is present.
</details>

audits.body:
Cloning https://aur.archlinux.org/youtube-to-mp3.git...

Analyzing youtube-to-mp3 AUR package with qwen/qwen3-235b-a22b-2507
Performing initial audit of PKGBUILD to ensure that we can safely run `makepkg`
LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD defines a single source for the x86_64 architecture, which is a Debian package downloaded from the official project website (mediahuman.com). The URL is consistent with the project's stated upstream and uses HTTPS, reducing the risk of tampering in transit. The source is a prebuilt binary (`.deb`), which will be extracted during later build steps, but no execution occurs during `makepkg --nobuild --nodeps --noprepare`.

The `pkgver()` function extracts the `control.tar.xz` from the downloaded `.deb` archive and reads the version from the `control` file. While `bsdtar -xf` is executed during sourcing of the PKGBUILD (because `pkgver()` is called), it only extracts files from the source that has just been downloaded — in this case, metadata from a Debian control archive. This is a common pattern for binary packages where version information is embedded in the upstream artifact. The operation does not involve remote code execution, dynamic payload fetching, or data exfiltration.

There are no signs of obfuscated commands, suspicious network calls, or malicious operations in the global scope or in `pkgver()`. The use of `sha256sums_x86_64` with a valid checksum ensures integrity of the source, though even if it were 'SKIP', that alone would not make this step unsafe per the gate criteria. Running `makepkg --nobuild --nodeps --noprepare` will safely fetch and extract sources and evaluate `pkgver()`, without executing any application code or running `prepare`/`build` phases.
</details>
<evidence>

</evidence>
<summary>
No malicious behavior in sourcing or source fetch
</summary>
</security_assessment>

LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD retrieves a prebuilt Debian package from the official project website (mediahuman.com) and extracts it using `bsdtar`. The source URL is specific to the declared upstream, and the checksum for the x86_64 `.deb` file is provided and matches standard practice. The `pkgver()` function reads the version from the embedded `control` file within the Debian metadata, which is a common and legitimate method when repackaging `.deb` files for Arch.

The `package()` function extracts the data archive, installs the license file, and creates a symlink in `/usr/bin`, all of which are standard operations for AUR packages that repackage binary distributions. No suspicious commands (e.g., `curl|bash`, `eval`, obfuscated scripts, or network calls during build) are present. The dependencies listed are typical Qt and multimedia libraries needed for GUI applications, consistent with the application's functionality.

Although the source is a prebuilt binary (which inherently limits auditability), this is not uncommon for closed-source applications distributed via AUR. There is no evidence of code injection, unexpected network activity, or malicious payload execution. The behavior aligns with normal repackaging workflows, and no red flags indicating supply chain compromise are present.
</details>
<evidence>

</evidence>
<summary>
Standard repackaging of trusted upstream binary; no malicious behavior detected.</summary>
</security_assessment>

LLM auditresponse for .SRCINFO:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The provided .SRCINFO file declares metadata for the youtube-to-mp3 package, including source URL and checksums. The source is a Debian package (`.deb`) hosted on the official project domain `mediahuman.com`, which matches the application's stated purpose. The checksum is explicitly defined using SHA-256, ensuring integrity verification during build. There are no signs of obfuscated commands, unexpected network operations, or execution of external scripts.

The package depends on standard multimedia and Qt libraries, consistent with a GUI-based media conversion tool. It does not introduce unsafe dependencies or system-wide modifications. The use of a prebuilt `.deb` from the vendor is a packaging choice that reduces transparency but does not constitute a supply-chain attack in itself, especially when paired with a verifiable checksum. No build or install instructions are present in this file, as expected for `.SRCINFO`.

While distributing prebuilt binaries in AUR packages limits auditability of the actual binary, this practice alone does not make the package unsafe — it is a known trade-off in the AUR ecosystem. Without evidence of code injection, data exfiltration, or unauthorized remote execution, the package metadata appears consistent with legitimate, albeit less-transparent, packaging practices.
</details>
<evidence>
